body: @Yay295 Would you please tell me why you thumbed down? Your opinion surely will improve the issue.

The purpose of `<rp>` is to provide a fallback if Ruby elements aren't supported. If Ruby elements *are* supported it shouldn't be visible. `<q>` is always visible. Also the semantics are different: `<rp>` represents fallback content, while `<q>` represents a quote.

@Yay295 Thank you a lot for response. I was afraid you were a troll and I'm sorry for that. I understand what you mean and now I'm sure `<rp>` and `<q>` is different in design.
I thought CSS should be responsible for the parenthesis presentation if rubies can't be rendered, but this is problematic when you want to copy the sentence because the words coalesce.

(FYI Chrome or Edge doesn't copy the `<rp>` element when you copied both `<ruby>` and `<rt>` with `<rp>` simultaneously while Firefox copies the starting parenthesis if you copy somewhere inside the `<rt>`. If you copy the `<ruby>` element and its outside, Chrome copies `<rt>` element successfully without `<rp>` and FF only copies ruby base text and ongoing text)

My main subject doesn't change much though: fallback isn't necessary now.

**Disclaimer: the below is based off of an amateur understanding and I would greatly appreciate any corrections from domain experts, such as @fantasai, @frivoal, or @whatwg/i18n.** My take on this is that the `` element is not well-documented in the spec. It says it's "to be shown by user agents that don't support ruby annotations", and it talks about how in "conforming user agents" it won't be rendered. So on first reading it does seem like, this is an element that should not exist, all modern browsers support ruby, and we should just get rid of it. We shouldn't be suggesting authors clutter their document with ``s, just like we don't suggest they clutter their document with `stuff`. (On the other hand, `

> It's also useful for giving the desired parentheses placement (or other fallback content) for plaintext-only contexts. A prominent example of such a context is pasting into a code editor, or "paste as plain text".

Note, tho, that the `rp` is display:none'd in supporting UAs, which means it's not put into the clipboard, and so wouldn't be useful for this case anyway.

> (e.g. ones that try to scrape existing content and use them to create flashcards automatically, while maintaining the plaintext storage format).

I'm not certain how this would work - if it's plaintext it won't want the markup, but if it doesn't have any markup then it's trivial to add parentheses at the same time as you're extracting the text. I suppose this lets people do text extraction with nothing more than a `.textContent` on the `ruby`, but this isn't something you can do generally anyway (if you're translating to plaintext, you'll want to add indicators for `em`/etc too, which have to be done manually).

I believe I'm on the same train, with `rp` being a funky legacy thing that we could relegate to the deprecated-but-supported section  now that ruby is widely supported, with just an `rp { display: none; }` required UA style rule.
Would `visibility: collapse` work better? I think that would allow it to be hidden but still selectable. It looks like only Firefox might support that right now though.

Also see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1801 where this was discussed in the context of the `innerText` getter. The special handling of `rp` (which was implemented in Gecko at the time) was removed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2129

q is poorly designed; IMHO deprecating rp would result in the same kind of poor design.

The whole purpose of rp is to mark up parentheses that will fall back correctly on browsers that don’t implement ruby (e.g., text browsers). If you take out all the tags, the resulting text is still valid. The reverse is useful when teaching HTML, because we can tell people that HTML is just normal text with markup added.

The problem with q is that using q requires the quotation marks to be removed, so q really isn’t markup. Similarly, if we depended on :before and :after to insert parentheses, it means we can’t start with a piece of text (e.g., a piece of news wire) and just add markup; we’ll have to remove text in order to make the result valid.

> If you take out all the tags, the resulting text is still valid. This is already violated by a number of HTML tags - as @NagayamaToshiaki says, `a` definitely qualifies, as does `sub`/`sup` (how many times have you seen something like `106` in a text version of a scientific PDF and had to realize it meant `106`?), a lot of the block elements like `li` or `details`, etc. HTML adds semantics to text; it is not necessarily *separable* from text, and we absolutely don't optimize for that naive "just display all the text content" case. If we did, then we'd have things like `10^6`, with user-agent CSS saying that if you support `sup` you should display:none a preceding `op` element; we'd have `
  • * first item`; we'd have `click here(http://example.com)`; etc. An actual text-only browser that wants to display HTML needs to know how to display textual equivalents of all the tags; such a browser can and *absolutely should* render `foobar` as "foo(bar)", without needing the author to add parens themselves; otherwise it would simply be broken. `rp` was a markup hack to handle inconsistent ruby support across rendering engines. It was clever, but it serves no useful purpose beyond that. We do not (and should not) recommend that people author their ruby with `rp` today. As far as I can tell, it can be safely relegated to the deprecated-but-supported appendix with other now-obsolete elements.

@NagayamaToshiaki `q` is terrible. It does not exhibit “graceful degradation” — a quality we used to highly value in HTML — and it’s absolutely the only element in HTML (maybe other than `table`) that behaves like this. Let me show you. Let’s start with this notice from the W3C’s home page: >The Web Real-Time Communications Working Group has published a First Public Working Draft of MediaStreamTrack Insertable Media Processing using Streams. To make it HTML you mark up the paragraph with tags (and in particular with `a`, which you claim to “not make sense”). That’s all. No deletions: >`

`The ``Web Real-Time Communications Working Group`` has published a First Public Working Draft of ``MediaStreamTrack Insertable Media Processing using Streams``.`

` This means if a researcher is writing a piece of ad hoc software that analyzes a collection of texts, the software can retrieve the plain text contents simply by stripping all tags away. You’d get exactly what you started with. q behaves completely differently. Consider this piece of source text: >According to the W3C, the Web Real-Time Communications Working Group “has published a First Public Working Draft of MediaStreamTrack Insertable Media Processing using Streams.” The sensible way to mark up the meaning of this sentence would be: >(*Invalid example*) `

`According to the W3C, the Web Real-Time Communications Working Group ``“has published a First Public Working Draft of MediaStreamTrack Insertable Media Processing using Streams.”`

` but it produces inconsistent results depending on what kind of browser you’re using and whether you’ve disabled the CSS for `q` (e.g., through reset.css). Instead, you need to *delete* the quotation marks: >`

`According to the W3C, the Web Real-Time Communications Working Group ``“has published a First Public Working Draft of MediaStreamTrack Insertable Media Processing using Streams.”`

` This produces correct results on recent browsers by default, but produces incorrect results if the CSS for `q` has been disabled (e.g., through reset.css), on text browsers, or on user agents that are not browsers (e.g., ad hoc research software written to analyze text content). There is absolutely no way to mark up a piece of text with `q` that produces consistent results. No matter how use `q`, some software will see quotation marks sometimes (even most of the time, but you can’t guarantee it); other software will never see any quotation marks. `rp` is a much better designed element. The whole purpose of `rp` is to provide “graceful degradation”. It does exactly what it was designed to do and the purpose is precisely to avoid the problem with `q`. (PS: One of the most well-known text browsers was written by a Japanese researcher. It’s sad to know text browsers are no longer well-known by Japanese people.)

@acli In my response (probably posted while you were writing yours), I list a number of common everyday HTML elements that fail your "graceful degradation" test exactly as much as `q` does. A "text browser" that literally just displays the raw text minus any tags would be fundamentally broken even on the simplest, most semantic realistic examples of pages. Such a browser needs to (and *does*, if I correctly recall my last brush with Lynx a decade ago) add textual equivalents to the default formatting each tag would provide in a graphical browser. `rp` is nearly the only (probably actually the only, but I'm rushed and don't want to scan down the full list of html elements) element in the entire HTML language that has this specific sort of "graceful degradation" behavior; HTML in general does not gracefully degrade to just its text content with no additional formatting, and was never intended to.

First, speaking of antiquated browser engines and no longer needing to worry about those: this is not nearly as much a thing of the past as this thread might imply. Yes, Gecko/Blink/Webkit all deal with ruby adequately enough. But command-line browsers like elinks or w3m don't. PDF formatters like [Prince](https://www.princexml.com/) don't. I believe [Flow](https://www.ekioh.com/flow-browser/) doesn't. [Servo](https://servo.org/) doesn't. I wouldn't bet that all EPUB readers do it properly either. All these still need fallback. Also, and possibly more importantly, a great number of things other than browsers that process HTML for variety of reasons don't have explicit ruby support. Without even going away from this site: the thing that makes table of contents from headings in github's markdown processor doesn't inject parentheses in the absence of rp. Other wiki engines don't fare better. Would you bet that the thing that extracts the name of spec editors to populate [specref](https://github.com/tobie/specref)'s database injects parentheses on its own? How about feed readers, aggregators, or scrapers of all kinds… We may want to argue that they all ought to deal with parenthesis injection, but way more often than not, they don't. So even if `` was only about fallback, it wouldn't be obsolete. However, that's not all it's for. The purpose of `` is to facilitate the linear rendering of ruby, which typically needs parentheses and the like to separate the various parts, since layout won't do that when you linearize. Linear rendering is indeed a good fallback for browsers/engines/contexts that don't support ruby, and it is indeed the appropriate thing to do for plaintext contexts which can only be linear, but it can also be a desirable deliberate stylistic choice even in contexts that would support ruby stacked layout. Often you want `明日（あした）` to look like , but sometimes you want it to look like 明日（あした）. Examples of reasons why you'd want to use a linear rendering deliberately: * A site with responsive design: at small font sizes, stacked ruby annotations get hard to read, so when the overall font-size of a document gets smaller than a certain point, the author may choose to linearize ruby * A site with responsive design: ruby requires a lot of space between the lines of text, and much of that space may be empty if not that many words are annotated with ruby. On small screens, the author may choose to linearize ruby to save space by reducing the interline leading. * Some people with dyslexia have trouble with ruby, so a site could offer a toggle between stacked ruby presentation or inline presentation, or a user stylesheet could do that as well. `` makes it easy to achieve such things. With that said, it is indeed more presentational markup than semantic markup, as you could largely infer the same information from the structure of the other ruby sub-elements and use generated content to inject the parentheses, but doing so without rp and relying on selectors, pseudos-elements and generated content isn't free of annoyances, even if you don't share https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7590#issuecomment-1035902098 's preferences. The browser engine will need to know of a way to generate the linearized version, and as an author, you'll need to independently do the same through selectors and generated content if you want your website to have a linear version for some of the reasons I highlighted above. But now you (or the browser engine, or both, depending on how you do it) will need to ensure that your injections don't interfere with the browser's generation of these same things, else you might end up with double parenthesis, for instance in copy-paste. Moreover, there is a measure of choice in the characters you use as the content of rp, and in the placement of the rp elements. Parentheses around (contiguous runs of) rt elements are typical. However, Unicode has a broad choice of parentheses or otherwise usable enclosing characters; you may want to include (or not) some spacing around things… Or you can decide to do something unusual, as shown in the second example of the spec in the [rp section](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/text-level-semantics.html#the-rp-element) (that's certainly contrieved, but that sort of thing isn't wrong). Anyways, if you do any of that using selectors and generated content rather than rp elements, none of the tools that generate parentheses when linearizing ruby will take advantage of that. Falling back to plain parentheses (or maybe to full-width parentheses? maybe in a language dependent way?) isn't semantically wrong, but it is unfortunate when the author had bothered to think of and supply a more tailored alternative. Also, If/when `` gets supported as well, `` can also come into play to support not just the separation between the base and the annotation, but also between consecutive annotations: For instance, take this Japanese example: ` 南欧(nan'o)` (meaning Southern Europe). “nano”, which is what you'd get out of rp-less markup (` 南欧nano`) would be an incorrect romanization, as that implies that the syllables are “na” and “no” rather than “nan” and “o”, as “nan'o” highlights. The same problem exists in in Chinese, where “xi'an” (the city of Xi'an) and “xian” (meaning "first") aren't the same. Unlike the parentheses, the presence or absence of a `'` could not generally be inferred from the structure of the markup, and depends on the actual textual content. I suppose if you used XPATH rather than css to get selectors that work on actual text, and encoded the phonology of various languages (and relied on content being language-tagged properly?), you might be able do without `` even in this case, but let's be realistic. To compound the challenge, look at this other Japanese example: `新大阪（Shin-Osaka）` (it means New Osaka, a train station). You need a separator to avoid misparsing shin+ō as “shinō” (which could be 死のう / let's die, or 市農 / city agriculture ) . But rather than the generic `'`, the separator here is conventionally `-`, because there's an understanding that 新大阪 is a compound of 新 and 大阪, so a hyphen is appropriate. Having to add classes or ids to `` elements so that you can chose between `'` or `-` or maybe a space or maybe nothing when injecting generated content is obnoxious when you could do that in markup with ``. And there's no way generic software is going to generate that for you when linearizing and get it right without information from the author in `` tags. ---- All in all, `` is a useful part of the markup that lets you conveniently support linearization of ruby and it's reasonable to use it in modern markup, particularly for fallback for antiquated or simplistic engines, but not only. ---- The questions about conversion-to-clipboard or the possible use of `visibility: collapse` are interesting ones, but that doesn't call for deprecating ``. I think *this* issue should be rejected and closed.

@frivoal I had no idea with rubying with alphabets/romaji and word break issue. I'm Japanese so I didn't notice of using rubies like that way.
But IMO this problem can be solved by using `<rt>`'s context because plain text in the `<ruby>`'s base text(or `<rb>`) and `<rt>` has one to one (or more `<rt>` to one ruby base text) connection, so transforming `<ruby><rb>新<rb>大<rb>阪<rt>Shin<rt>O<rt>saka</ruby>` or `<ruby><rb>西</rb><rb>安</rb><rt>xi</rt><rt>an</rt></ruby>` is complex but not too difficult, if browsers handle those like: 
- For the former, when there's `<rt>` next to another `<rt>` and the first ends with "n" and the second starts with vowels (either "a", "e", "i", "o", "u") add "-" or "'".
- For the latter, when two `<rt>`s are continuing and the first ends with vowels (now adding "er") and the other starts with them, add "'".
- To accomplish those interpretations, adding `lang` attribute somewhere is necessary. It should be added to `<ruby>` (unless `<ruby>` is the `<html>`'s language).

Rather, you shouldn't stick on `<rb>` because it is deprecated (I think the element should be back to spec though: see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7587) and write those with new syntax: `<ruby>新大阪<rt>Shin-Osaka</rt></ruby>` or `<ruby>西<rt>xi</rt></ruby><ruby>安<rt>an</rt></ruby>`.

Thanks @frivoal for the excellent post; this is exactly what I was hoping for. I tend to agree that this indicates we should leave the spec as-is, perhaps with some additional content to make it clearer for future readers. However, the most compelling argument against ``, which I'm not sure you addressed directly, was @tabatkins discussion about whether this is a general pattern. He said: > HTML adds semantics to text; it is not necessarily _separable_ from text, and we absolutely don't optimize for that naive "just display all the text content" case. If we did, then we'd have things like `10^6`, with user-agent CSS saying that if you support `sup` you should display:none a preceding `op` element; we'd have `
  • * first item`; we'd have `click here(http://example.com)`; etc. An actual text-only browser that wants to display HTML needs to know how to display textual equivalents of all the tags; such a browser can and _absolutely should_ render `foobar` as "foo(bar)", without needing the author to add parens themselves; otherwise it would simply be broken. I'd love to hear more about your take on this: - Is ruby just more special than superscripts or links or bullets, such that it benefits more from the textual fallback than those do? - Or maybe you think that having such textual fallback for superscripts/links/bullets would be a good idea, and it's mostly a historical accident that ruby markup got one baked in, and those didn't? My tentative take is that a lot of the complexities you mention are pointing toward the former. But I'm not sure, and would love to hear more explicitly. E.g., the choice as to whether your textual fallback is `10^66` or `10⁶6` seems like a similar author choice to your choice-of-parenthesis-character. Or, the idea that responsive design sites might want a linearized `10^6` instead of a taller `106` seems similar to the considerations for ruby. So it's not immediately clear to me that ruby is extra-special in this regard.

For what it’s worth, `<sup>` was in HTML 0.9. It’s so old that not having a fallback form is almost irrelevant. If a piece of software decides to do something about `<sup>`, they have no excuse in not knowing about `<sup>`; and if it knows it’s only dealing with superscripted digits, we have superscripted digits in Unicode. A lot of software don’t care, and the humans that need to deal with the resulting garbage output (translators and copy editors, for example) don’t know enough about the problem to care. `<sup>` becomes a real problem when what’s inside the `sup` element is complex or not entirely digits; superscripted ordinal endings or other superscripted suffixes (still mainstream in French, for example), for example, will not be dealt with correctly.

On the other hand, `<rp>` is relatively new. How many pieces of software (other than the main GUI browser engines) know about `<rp>`? Why do we assume when any new tag is added to HTML, all software in existence will need to be updated to deal with the new tag?

(For what it’s worth, in an ideal world, the fallback for `<sup>` should not always be `^`. For example, if the superscript is a note number, having `(Note ` and `)` for fallback would have been much more appropriate, both from a text browser POV and from a screen reader POV. Yes, I’m arguing that `<sup>` should have been designed with the equivalent of an `<rp>` but as I mentioned, `<sup>` is old, it was in HTML 0.9. We’re supposed to be wiser after more than 20 years of HTML.)

We used to call this “black magic”. We used to know minimizing “black magic” was a good thing. And now we’re discussing why we need to drop a machine-readable hint because we feel black magic is better than having a hint. 

Okay, I’ve talked too much. I’ll unsubscribe from this discussion.

ETA: “Robustness” is still a W3C design principle. We often talk about robustness as if it’s only the content creator/generator’s job, but I’ll argue here that it goes both ways. Removing `rp` is an assault on robustness because doing this is to actively cause unknown software to fail.

> For what it’s worth, `sup` was in HTML 0.9. It’s so old that not having a fallback form is almost irrelevant.

You say that, but copy-pasting from an HTML document still results in messed up plain text. `10<sup>6</sup>` becomes `106` when pasted, despite its nearly three-decade pedigree.  So the point isn't "old well-supported markup" vs "newer less-supported markup"; one of the problems `rp` is theoretically aiming to solve is still present across all of HTML. (And it doesn't solve that problem anyway, as stated previously; copy/pasting from a document with ruby still linearizes the text without `rp` added.)

> On the other hand, <rp> is relatively new. How many pieces of software (other than the main GUI browser engines) know about <rp>? Why do we assume when any new tag is added to HTML, all software in existence will need to be updated to deal with the new tag?

Not really. Ruby has been part of HTML for over a decade; the markup structure hasn't significantly changed in this regard since it was added, iirc. [Per CanIUse](https://caniuse.com/ruby), it's had at least partial support for about a decade across browser engines. (I don't wanna track down exactly when it was added to the HTML spec, but XHTML Ruby was first published back in 2001.)

-----

Regarding formatting, I'll note that the use of `rp` for inter-group annotations like dash or apostrophe is also display, not semantic; you'd want the separator displayed in stacked ruby *if* you were using jukugo layout and the bases merged their annotations, but not otherwise. So ideal layout is still more complicated than `rp`'s "never display when stacked, always display when linear" rule.

> `rp` is nearly the only (probably actually the only, but I'm rushed and don't want to scan down the full list of html elements) element in the entire HTML language that has this specific sort of "graceful degradation" behavior; HTML in general does not gracefully degrade to just its text content with no additional formatting, and was never intended to.

Are `<iframe>` and `<canvas>` examples of elements that gracefully degrade to text (whatever the author types between the opening and closing tags)?

> However, the most compelling argument against ``, which I'm not sure you addressed directly, was @tabatkins discussion about whether this is a general pattern. He said: > > > HTML adds semantics to text; it is not necessarily _separable_ from text, and we absolutely don't optimize for that naive "just display all the text content" case. If we did, then we'd have things like `10^6`, with user-agent CSS saying that if you support `sup` you should display:none a preceding `op` element; we'd have `
  • * first item`; we'd have `click here(http://example.com)`; etc. An actual text-only browser that wants to display HTML needs to know how to display textual equivalents of all the tags; such a browser can and _absolutely should_ render `foobar` as "foo(bar)", without needing the author to add parens themselves; otherwise it would simply be broken. > > I'd love to hear more about your take on this: > > * Is ruby just more special than superscripts or links or bullets, such that it benefits more from the textual fallback than those do? > > * Or maybe you think that having such textual fallback for superscripts/links/bullets would be a good idea, and it's mostly a historical accident that ruby markup got one baked in, and those didn't? Mainly the former, because linearization of ruby is not only a fallback for insufficiently capable UAs, but occasionally a deliberate stylistic choice. Examples: * Ruby takes a lot of vertical space. So if you want consistent vertical rhythm, you need a fairly big line-height. If you've got ruby on comparatively few words, that could feel like a lot of wasted real estate. So on a small screen, you might switch to the the linearized/parenthesized version to save space. * Ruby text is smaller than its base. If the base text itself gets rendered in a very small font size for some reason, there's a risk that ruby displayed as ruby could be to small to read, and that it would be preferable to switch to the linear rendering. * Ruby confused some people with dyslexia, who instead of seeing a helpful annotation on top of a possibly unknown letter, will visually process the combination as a giant unknown thing, and not know what to do with it. Such users can prefer ruby to be rendered linearized/parenthesized version. Because such choices can be contextual (like the first one) or user preferences (like the second one), we still benefit from having markup that carries the full correct semantics, including `` tags to support the author's prefered linearization, and being able to dynamically switch based on Media queries, container queries, in-site user settings, e-reader user settings…

> On the other hand, `<rp>` is relatively new. 

It's as old as the rest of the HTML ruby model (and all its variants), closing in on 25 years: https://www.w3.org/TR/1998/WD-ruby-19981221/

Don't forget the existence of text-based browsers. Text-based browsers matter.

If you strip extra tags in a HTML content in your program (e.g. sanitizer), the content in `<rp>` should be respected and kept even if `<rp>` itself were removed.

I wanted to highlight a use case that doesn't seem to have come up explicitly yet: **Search Engine Result Page title links and snippets on Google, Bing, Yahoo!, etc**. This seems like a concrete instance of the "scrapers" case @frivoal mentioned above.

When these search engines generate title links and description snippets for pages that use `<ruby>`, they don't render ruby properly. Instead, they flatten the base text and the `<rt>` annotation together. Without `<rp>`, the base text and its reading end up concatenated with no separator, which makes the result confusing or even unreadable. With `<rp>`, at least the annotation appears in parentheses, which is far more legible.

This is a very high‑traffic, everyday scenario — arguably the single most common real‑world case where `<rp>` fallback is actually seen by end users — so I think it's worth considering in this discussion.
